lines.note: This completes the preceding page's Monozuqi definition: an inclination to make and possess novel, curious things. The physical row starts with fazer; the preceding page's catchword is not a second body occurrence.
Monpa names a religious branch or sect; the Portuguese gives religion or sect. It begins a new flush-left entry rather than continuing the preceding definition.
Monqen is explained through seeing and hearing (mi and qiqu). The Portuguese likewise gives ver and ouuir, then introduces the next row's example. The headword is flush-left.
The example asserts that there is no uncertainty in what is seen or heard. The slightly broken u in maguire remains legible, and the Portuguese ou- continues as uir on the next row.

runs.text: uir, não hà que duuidar, ou o que he hum homẽ

lines.note: This continues ou-uir and says that there is nothing to doubt. The apparently awkward printed sequence o que he hum homẽ is retained, including the abbreviated nasal ending, rather than silently rewriting its syntax.

runs.text: vè, & ouue, he couſa clara, & ſem duuida.

lines.note: The explanation concludes that what a person sees and hears is clear and beyond doubt. The original vè, ouue and duuida spellings and the supplied accent reading are retained.
Monriǔ denotes a school or sect, matching the brief Portuguese gloss. The marked final vowel is worn but supports the supplied ǔ; this is a new entry, not an indented continuation.
Monſai combines knowledge of letters with practical intelligence. Both Japanese explanatory words remain roman, and the Portuguese sentence continues with prudencia below.
The Portuguese completes the pairing of learning and prudence; the Japanese example describes a person with these qualities in abundance. The example continues through nari on the next line.

runs.text: He homem de muitas letras, & pru

lines.note: Nari closes the Japanese assertion. Its translation calls the person learned and prudent. There is no visible terminal hyphen after pru, so none is supplied merely because dencia follows.
This short row completes prudencia from the preceding row. The upright S. is the dictionary's written-usage label, distinct from the italic Portuguese word.

runs.text: Porteiro, guarda, ou vigia da porta.

lines.note: Monſu names a gatekeeper, matching porteiro, guarda and vigia da porta. The long-s form is retained and the entry starts flush-left.
Montai is glossed as lettering, form or painting. The apparent t and following a agree with the repeated Montaiga below; no modernization of the headword is made.

The Japanese example says that the writing or design cannot be seen. The Portuguese begins the equivalent statement that it is no longer visible and continues on the next row; the paragraph sign is present.

runs.text: letra nem pintura, tudo eſtà apagado.

lines.note: The translation concludes that neither lettering nor painting is visible because everything has faded or been erased. The supplied eſtà allograph and grave are retained.

runs.text: Seita, ou os profeßores dalgũa ſeita.

lines.note: Montei denotes a sect or its adherents here. The β-shaped ligature in profeßores and the nasal abbreviation in dalgũa are preserved rather than expanded.
The example names the members of a sect or school. Monteino xu is roman Japanese, while the introducing Vt, is italic; this belongs to Montei above.
Monteixi means disciples or adherents, as the Portuguese explains. The two tall s-types in profeſſores differ from the ligature in the earlier Montei entry and are kept separately.
This completes the phrase referring to adherents of a sect. The final S. is upright and marks written usage, not part of the italic gloss.
Monto again denotes a sect or its followers. The abbreviated dalgũa is not expanded, and this independent headword remains flush-left.

runs.text: Caſca que fica da cegarrega, ou cor-

lines.note: Monuqe is the empty shell left by a cicada, which the Portuguese describes as a shell or apparently dead body. The visible cor- continues as po on the following row; cegarrega is retained as printed.

runs.text: po morto com figura, olhos, &c. como que ſe

lines.note: The shell retains the body's shape and eyes. The row completes corpo and begins the comparison with a living cicada; the original conditional wording como que ſe is retained.
The comparison ends with the cicada seeming alive. A paragraph introduces Monuqeno coromo, divided physically after co-; the Japanese phrase stays roman.

The phrase refers to an empty garment in poetic usage. The scan has parentheses around Apud Poëtas, not the OCR paragraph sign, and two distinct dots over e support Poëtas rather than Poẽtas. The Portuguese definition continues at po-sto.

runs.text: sto de feição, como que eſtà dentro alguem ve-

lines.note: The garment is arranged as though someone were inside it. A tall t-stroke is visible in eſtà, correcting the OCR eſà; the printed ve- joins ſtido below. The existing st/ſt distinction is otherwise retained.

runs.text: ſtido, ou deitado, mas não he mais que apa-

lines.note: The apparent occupant is dressed or lying down, but is only an appearance. Enlarging the damaged word shows the ascender of d and the sequence supporting deitado, not OCR ãeitado; its middle types are weak. The hyphen in apa- remains.
This completes aparencia and closes the comparison with a seemingly occupied but actually empty garment. It is a continuation, not a separate entry.

runs.text: Proua, ou autoridade eſcrita que ſe

lines.note: Monxô is cited written evidence or authority. The circumflex over the headword's final o is visible; a worn d in autoridade does not warrant deleting that letter.

runs.text: alega pera confirmar algũa questão, verda-

lines.note: The written authority is adduced to confirm a question or truth. The historical pera and algũa are kept, and the physical verda- continues below.
This completes verdade and ends the definition of documentary authority. The short row and its original continuation placement are retained.

runs.text: Homem que està vigiando a porta

lines.note: Monyacu names a man assigned to watch the gate. The headword ends in cu, and the Portuguese qualification continues on the following row.
The gatekeeper is said to be commonly of low status. Commumente, he and baixo are copied as printed rather than modernized.
Monyô first means relatives through any connection; the paragraph introduces an additional meaning below. The headword has a circumflex and the Portuguese Itẽ retains its abbreviation.

runs.text: Os que pertencem à meſma ſeita. Vt,

lines.note: The second sense is people belonging to the same sect. The example begins with the abbreviated Mõ- and continues yôno; its tilde must not be regularized to the headword's vowel mark.
This completes the example referring to the people of a shared lineage or sect. The circumflex belongs to yô, and the following upright S. marks written usage.
Moppara and mopparana are paired alternative forms, glossed as necessary and, on the next row, important. The two p-types are distinct and the linking l, remains roman.

The example concerns making virtue one's chief concern. The scan supports consonantal initial I in Ienuo, not a normalized Z; the following Portuguese virtue gloss supplies the lexical context. This is an indented continuation of Moppara.

runs.text: Fazer muito caſo, ou exercitar ſempre a vir-

lines.note: The Portuguese interprets the example as valuing virtue greatly or continually practising it. The line is indented and the printed vir- continues below.
This completes virtude in the preceding example's translation. The short row stays with Moppara and is restored to continuation indentation.
Mopparani is the adverbial form of the preceding entry. The scan has r rather than OCR t in the final sequence, and the grammatical label Adu. is italic.
The verb means to gain or acquire. The headword's small mark points down like the clear carons in the following examples, so Mǒqe replaces OCR Môqe; the printed aquirir is not modernized to adquirir.
The example means to have a child, translated as a child being born to someone. Enlarged letterforms give alguem and filho, correcting the OCR aljuem and fibo; Nacer remains as printed.
The noun denotes gain or profit; the example contrasts having and not having it. Both marked o-vowels are carons, and the alternative marker l, stays roman.
This translates the positive and negative alternatives about profit. The second auer has weak ink in u but remains recoverable from the visible traces; the row is an indented continuation.
Mǒqen is explained as seeing indiscriminately or wrongly. The Japanese synonym stays roman; the Portuguese nasal abbreviation in deſordẽ is preserved.

runs.text: ou errar no ver, & eſpecular as couſas da ſal-

lines.note: The gloss extends the error to seeing and contemplating matters of salvation. It is a continuation, with the original ſal- break retained.
This completes ſaluação and closes the entry. The final S. is upright, while the Portuguese fragment is italic; the row is indented rather than a new flush-left item.

Môqet and qe ana designate bodily pores. Enlargement shows a rounded first vowel with a grave in Pòros, not the OCR Pèros; the damaged contour is recoverable. The headword is flush-left and final S. upright.

runs.text: Malenconia, ou triſteza por morte de

lines.note: This Môqi means grief or melancholy after a death. Its circumflex distinguishes it from the separate Mǒqi below; the definition continues with the relatives in the next row.
The first sense concerns grief for parents or children; the paragraph then adds illness. The historical pay and the italic example label remain as printed.

The polite example describes an honoured person's illness. A circumflex is visible over the second o in Gomôqide, omitted by OCR. The scan supports algua without a securely visible nasal mark, so no n or tilde is supplied.
This completes the Portuguese explanation: an honoured person being ill. It belongs to the courteous Japanese formula on the preceding row.
This distinct Mǒqi means a blind turtle, with the Japanese paraphrase Mexijta came. The caron and the small terminal stop after olhos are visible; the entry starts flush-left.
The paragraph introduces a request for assistance through the blind-turtle comparison. The omitted paragraph sign is restored, gocôriocuuo keeps its circumflex, and fu- continues bocuto below.
The Japanese request treats the addressee's help like floating wood available to the blind turtle. The Portuguese begins the corresponding request for aid; the ligature in voßa is preserved.

runs.text: com que me ſocorrais como pao a que ſe pega a

lines.note: The requested assistance is compared to the wood to which a turtle clings. The narrow internal types of ſocorrais are somewhat worn, but the aligned reading is retained without adding a consonant; pao is not modernized.
This closes the comparison with the blind turtle. The row contains the end of the preceding request, not a second definition of the animal.

runs.text: O tomar a pena pera eſcreuer. Vt,

lines.note: Môqio is taking up the pen to write. The headword's circumflex and the historical pena and pera remain; the italic Vt, introduces the following example.
The example says there is no leisure to take up the pen. The Portuguese translation continues on the next row, and no extra punctuation is inferred from the small isolated speck near the right edge.
This completes the translation as having no time to write. The italic fragment remains attached to the Môqio example.

The verb means to ask or beg; the example concerns asking for alms. The printed initial I and following f in Iifiuo are retained, as are the carons in the principal forms and morǒ. No stop is supplied at the open right edge.
This translates Iifiuo morǒ as asking for alms. The singular eſmola is retained and the row is a continuation of the verb entry.

runs.text: O chegarſe a ouuir o que outros

lines.note: Moraiguiqi describes coming close to hear what others are saying. The gui-qi sequence is visible and matches the repeated example below; the definition continues on the following line.
The people are speaking or disputing; the Japanese example means engaging in this attentive listening. Worn rounded types in the repeated Moraiguiqiuo do not justify changing its vowels.

runs.text: O chorar com ver a outros cho

lines.note: Morainaqi is crying on seeing others cry. Enlargement of the final damaged type shows the tall stem and faint lower/shoulder traces compatible with h, so cho replaces OCR clo; this remains a nonblocking damaged-glyph reading. No terminal hyphen is visible.
This completes chorar and gives the Japanese verbal example for sympathetic crying. The roman phrase and italic Vt, are kept distinct.
The transitive verb means to let something escape. Enlargement of the crowded right edge reveals the full final r of deixar, not the OCR hyphen in deixa-; the word is complete on this row.
The example describes drawing fish into a net without letting any escape. The circumflex on Xôguio and the attached particles are retained, and the Japanese sentence continues below.

runs.text: Meter na rede ſem deixar eſca-

lines.note: Fiqi iruru completes the action of drawing into the net. The Portuguese translation continues with the visible eſca- break at the right edge.

runs.text: par nem os peixinhos. ¶ Item, Deſcobrir

lines.note: Not even the little fish escape. A new paragraph adds the meaning of disclosing something, leading into the secret on the next line; no body row is omitted between the senses.

The additional sense is revealing a secret, illustrated by a Japanese phrase about making secret matters known outside. The printed fimituo and the mo- break are retained, without expanding the romanization.

This completes the disclosure example, then begins a further expression concerning seminal emission. The supplied grave on raſù is weak in this impression and is retained provisionally rather than inferred afresh; mo- continues below.

runs.text: Ter polução, ou derramar a ſemente.

lines.note: The phrase is glossed as having an emission or spilling semen. The anatomical euphemism ſemente is retained literally, and this raſu has no supplied accent.
This intransitive verb means to escape or slip away, contrasting with the preceding transitive Moraxi. The crowded italic Vt, at the right rule introduces the example below.
The example describes a small fish escaping a net. The unusual but visible Covuoua is retained, and its Portuguese subject continues into the next row's predicate.
The first translation says the fish escapes the net. A new example concerns departing from reason, with the Portuguese Diſ- continued on the following line.
This completes Diſcrepar da razão and adds Moreqicoyuru, becoming known by being heard. The next Portuguese definition begins with the visible Deſ- line break.
The additional sense is a secret thing becoming disclosed or heard about. The initial letter of ſecreta lacks the f crossbar and matches the nearby long-s types, correcting OCR fecreta.
Mǒret is explained as fierce or severe through Taqecu and qibixij. There is no word-space inside qibixij; the false OCR split is removed. The headword's caron is clear.
This completes the description with harshness or severity. The historical riſpido spelling is retained; final S. is upright and indicates written usage.
This Mori denotes a guardian or tutor and also a watcher. A second paragraph introduces the honorific Vonmori, divided after Von- at the line edge.
Vonmori is glossed as the tutor or guardian of a noble person. The split honorific form is not mistaken for a new headword, and peßoa retains its ligature.
This independent homograph means a wood or grove. Its short complete definition is kept separate from the preceding guardian sense and the following leak sense.

runs.text: Goteira que caye do telhado. Vt,

lines.note: This Mori is water dripping from a roof. The example begins Mo- with a clear horizontal hyphen, correcting OCR Mo.; it continues riga below.
The example says that a drip fell on something or someone. The visible cacatta and abbreviated hũa are retained; the row is an indented continuation, not a new entry.
The verb means to drip, and the paragraph adds leaking from a vessel. The worn right-edge al- is retained, completing algum with the next row.
This completes algum vaſo in the explanation of a leaking vessel. It remains an indented continuation of the preceding verb.
This homographic verb concerns serving food, rather than leaking. The headword's r is worn but recoverable, and the Japanese example begins Mexiuo before continuing below.

runs.text: Tirar, & por o comer nos Goquis.

lines.note: Mexiuo moru means serving rice or food. The explanation specifies placing it in Goquis; this Japanese vessel-name is embedded within Portuguese and is marked for optional typeface review. The line is indented.

runs.text: Comer, ou outra couſa posta em

lines.note: Morimono is food or another thing placed in a vessel. The existing italic posta is retained without imposing a new st-ligature classification; the definition continues below.

Goqui and Chauan name the vessels within the Portuguese definition, so both are typeface-review terms. The paragraph then begins a separate Japanese example; its words are not embedded Portuguese terms. The row is a continuation.
The example concerns spilling something while serving it. The scan reads Entornar, with n after E, correcting OCR Eintornar; the joined historical deitandoa is retained.

This completes the reference to porcelain or a Goqui vessel. Porſolana remains in its printed spelling, while Goqui is a Japanese noun embedded in Portuguese and is marked for optional typeface review.

This final Mori is a defective verb meaning to guard or watch. The entry continues beyond this page; the isolated ¶ Ruſu below is furniture, not a further body row. No terminal stop is supplied from indistinct edge specks.

zones.label: Printed catchword

lines.note: The isolated far-right paragraph sign and Ruſu are a catchword for the continuation of the final guard/watch entry, not an extra physical body row. The next page was not supplied, so its continuation has not been independently checked.
